channel.title: AI, Honestly
channel.description: Ideas about AI, without the hype. Essays on where AI is heading, and working papers that put ideas to the test.

item.title: Borrowed Time
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, November 2026. A short essay about us and the machines we are building. Where I give a fact, I give the source; where I borrow an idea from physics, I say how far the comparison goes. The figures are drawings of my own, the second after a known result from physics. The code that draws them is linked under each one.

In short. A mathematician and an AI have proved the Riemann hypothesis, as reported, and a computer has checked every step. Written out, the proof would run past 250,000 pages, and nobody can read it yet. That raises questions worth asking. Is searching a way of thinking? Maybe understanding is search, paid for in advance. Our brain paid with time, and now learns all its life on about twenty watts. Our machines pay with time borrowed from everything people ever wrote, and with power. Soon, other machines will shorten the proof and explain it. But every mind pays for its own understanding, and it pays at human speed. So I propose another view of progress. No proof without a reader. Big models that explore, and small ones, close to us, that teach. And time to understand.

1. What is a proof for?

On 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, announced that he and Claude, the company’s AI, had proved the Riemann hypothesis (Scientific American 2026). It is a question about the prime numbers, open for 167 years. The proof is written in Lean, a language in which a computer checks every step. The next day, as reported, the Lean and Mathlib communities certified that it is correct (Technology.org 2026). Written out in prose, it ran past 250,000 pages, and he chose not to post it (OfficeChai 2026). I wrote about that day in Long First, Short Later.

Read one page a minute, eight hours a day, and you would need a year and a half. So here is a truth, perhaps the most wanted in mathematics, in a book that no person will read. Even the certificate says that mathematicians still have work to do to explain the proof’s ideas. The journal Science put the question in its headline: can humans understand the answer (Science 2026)?

So, what is a proof for? To know that something is true, or to understand why? Today we have the first. Not yet the second.

In 1953, the philosopher Martin Heidegger closed a lecture on technology with a line I keep coming back to. “Questioning,” he wrote, “is the piety of thought” (Heidegger 1977). Piety here means a kind of respect. He asked us neither to reject technology nor to follow it blindly, but to keep questioning it. So this essay is a series of questions, each with a proposal. Not verdicts.

2. Is searching a way of thinking?

It is tempting to say that the machine only searches, so fast that it looks like thinking. I am no longer sure that is enough. These systems now find things nobody had found (Partly Wrong, Mostly Right). And what is a discovery, if not a search that ends somewhere new? In 1976, Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, two founders of the field, proposed that intelligence is search, guided by good rules of thumb (Newell and Simon 1976). If so, the question is not whether a machine searches. It is how the search was paid for.

Chess gives a clue. In 1997, Deep Blue beat the world champion by examining well over a hundred million positions every second (Campbell et al. 2002). Decades earlier, the psychologist Adriaan de Groot had asked strong players to think aloud. The grandmasters did not look at more moves than weaker players. They looked at a handful, and saw the good ones first (de Groot 1965). Then, in 2017, AlphaZero beat the strongest chess program of the time while looking at about a thousand times fewer positions (Silver et al. 2018). It had not escaped the search. It had moved it: millions of games against itself, played before the match, in training.

Here is the view I propose. Understanding is search, paid for in advance. The grandmaster paid with years of games. AlphaZero paid in a data centre. We could never try everything, so we had to understand.

That is where understanding starts, not where it ends. Paid-for search gives a feel for the right move. AlphaZero has that feel, but it cannot tell you why a move is good. A grandmaster can. Understanding why is that feel put into words that someone else can follow.

3. What made us?

Nobody designed the human brain. Selection did: hundreds of millions of years of small changes, most of them failures. It was not cheap. Evolution ran on the sunlight of the whole living world, through billions of lives. But the cost was spread so thin, over so much time, that each step was almost free. Then each of us added a childhood.

What it left is small. Everything we inherit at birth is written in about three billion letters of DNA (Nurk et al. 2022), less than a gigabyte by my count. A child learns language from fewer than a hundred million words heard by the age of thirteen, by researchers’ estimates (Warstadt et al. 2023). And the brain does all this on about twenty watts, a small light bulb (Raichle and Gusnard 2002; Balasubramanian 2021). It does not only think on twenty watts. It learns on twenty watts, every day of its life.

The researcher François Chollet proposed measuring intelligence just this way. Not by what a system can do, but by how little experience it needs to learn it (Chollet 2019). What if we measured our machines like that too? By that measure, the child is still far ahead. That seems to me a goal worth aiming at.

4. What if data is time?

Time made us in three ways. The time evolution took to design us, the time a childhood takes to fill a brain, and the slowness of thinking itself. Each time, nature spread its energy thin over time, instead of spending it all at once. We want the same mind without the wait. But I don’t think time vanishes when we skip it. We pay for it in another currency.

Look at training data as time. Llama 3, an open model from 2024, was trained on more than fifteen trillion tokens, the small pieces of words these models read (Meta 2024). By my own count, that is roughly a hundred thousand times what a child hears by thirteen. Every page of it was written by a person, over centuries. So we did not really skip the time. We borrowed it. Data is time, stored. That is not a reproach. It is a gift from everyone who ever wrote, and it deserves to be used well.

Then we add power. The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres used about one and a half percent of the world’s electricity in 2024. It expects that to more than double by 2030, mostly because of AI (International Energy Agency 2025). I must be careful here. One trained model is shared by millions of people, so counted per answer, it can be cheap. The point is that building these minds fast gathers, in one place, what nature spread over ages.

Physics has a name for this trade. A process run very slowly can waste almost nothing; run it faster, and it wastes more. In 1975, Frank Curzon and Boris Ahlborn showed what this means for an engine. Run it for the most power, and it is much less efficient than it could be. Push it faster still, and you get less power, not more (Curzon and Ahlborn 1975).

Chips sit on the fast side. They switch billions of times a second, and switching faster costs more energy (Horowitz 2014). The brain took the other side. On average, a neuron fires only a few times a second (Attwell and Laughlin 2001). It is slow and parallel, and it keeps its memory next to its computing. A chip does not, and fetching a number from memory costs it over a hundred times the energy of a multiplication (Horowitz 2014).

So nature paid in time, and we pay in borrowed time and power. Neither is free. The question is which we can afford, and for what.

5. What do we gain by going faster?

If we could shrink that time to almost nothing, what would we really gain, as human beings? Often, a lot. Innovation is not the enemy, and physics agrees: an engine run infinitely slowly gives no power at all. When a disease spreads, every month saved is lives saved.

But past a certain speed, an engine gives less. An engine is not a society, and I use it as an image, not a proof. Still, it invites a question. Could we go past that speed too?

Look at the proof again. Other models can read the 250,000 pages, find the steps that matter, write a shorter proof, and explain it as many times as we ask. I believe that will happen soon. The prime number theorem waited 84 years for its four-page proof. This time, the wait may be months.

But here the idea from chess comes back. If understanding is search paid for in advance, someone has to pay. The machine has paid for its own understanding of the proof, and it can even put it into words. That does not pay for ours. Every mind pays for its own understanding. A good explanation lowers the price, sometimes by a lot. But nobody can pay it for us, and we pay at human speed.

So the slow part moves. Producing explanations used to be slow. Now, taking them in is. A thousand clear explanations a day help nobody if nobody has the time to read one. And we are not always good judges of our own speed. In one small experiment in 2025, experienced programmers using AI tools took 19 percent longer, yet felt about 20 percent faster (Becker et al. 2025). A good reason to measure, rather than assume.

6. Which AI do we want beside us?

I am not against AI. I use it in my work every day. So my question is not “big or small?” It is this one: which AI lowers the price of understanding, for one person?

That is what a good tutor does. It knows what you already understand, notices where you are lost, and waits. In 1984, the educational researcher Benjamin Bloom reported that the average student taught one to one did better than about ninety-eight percent of a class (Bloom 1984). Later reviews found a smaller gain, but still a large one, and found that good computer tutors came close to human ones (VanLehn 2011).

I believe a small brain, close to us, could be that tutor. It does not need to know everything. It needs to know one person well, and stay with them. On their phone or their desk, it would learn where they live, the way a brain does. I sketched such a local mind in An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle and Fast AI. The big and the small need not compete. One can be the explorer. The other can be the guide who walks home with you.

7. Three proposals

So, instead of a verdict, three proposals.

No proof without a reader. When a machine finds a result, let us call the work finished only when at least one person can explain it in their own words. Count understanding, not only answers.

Let the big models explore, and the small ones teach. Build both, for different jobs. The frontier finds and shortens. The companion close to us helps one person understand, at their pace.

Give understanding its own time. For every answer a machine gives us quickly, keep some time to take it in: to read, to doubt, to explain it back. That time is not lost. It is how borrowed time gets repaid.

More than a century ago, the poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote to a young man who wanted answers. He told him to be patient with what is still unsolved, and to “live the questions now”. Perhaps then, he wrote, one day you will live your way into the answer (Rilke 1934).

Time made a mind that learns on twenty watts. We are building minds on borrowed time. I don’t know the right speed. But I think it is a question worth living, not a race worth winning.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.

The views in this essay are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

item.title: The Disposable Screen
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, November 2026. A short and deliberately provocative essay about the screens we build for software, and why they will matter much less than they do today. It is a bet, not a forecast with numbers. Where I state a fact, I give the source. The three figures are drawings of my own, and the code that draws them is linked under each one.

In short. We spend months designing screens for our software, and each person then uses a small part of them. That effort is about to lose most of its reason. A screen exists so that a person can drive the backend by hand: the functions that do the work, and the data they use. An AI agent drives those functions directly. For most tasks, no screen is needed at all. When a person must see something or decide, the agent draws a screen for that moment. It shows the facts and the one button the decision needs, and then it is thrown away. The generic screen, defined in advance and the same for everyone, stops being the centre of software. Habit, trust and the need to explore will keep some fixed screens alive, but they will be the exception. What matters now is the backend, described well, and the rules about what a person must always see.

1. The screen nobody needed

Today, building software is, for a large part, building screens. Teams run workshops, draw mock-ups, test with users and argue about where a button goes. The result is coded page by page and maintained for years.

Then watch what happens. One person opens the screen to change an address. Another approves one invoice. A third exports a report once a quarter. Each one touches a few fields and one button. The rest is there for someone else.

So the screen is a compromise: one drawing, defined in advance, for everyone and every task. For the average user it may be the best interface. For any one person on any one day, most of it is useless.

2. The screen was only the way in

A screen is not the software. It is a way in. Behind every button sits a function in the backend: find this invoice, check that supplier, send this payment. The screen exists because, until now, a person had to drive those functions by hand, one click at a time.

That is ending. In November 2024, Anthropic published the Model Context Protocol, an open standard that lets an AI agent find and call the functions of other systems (Anthropic 2024b). A service describes its functions as data: what each one does, what it needs, what it returns. I wrote about this in The Interface Is Data. The agent reads the description and calls the functions itself. No menu, no page, no form.

Jakob Nielsen, who has studied usability for decades, saw the shift coming in 2023. He called AI the first new way of using computers in sixty years: you say what you want, and the machine works out how (Nielsen 2023). Satya Nadella, the head of Microsoft, went further at the end of 2024. He described most business applications as databases with business rules on top, and said those rules are moving to agents (Windows Central 2024). If so, what remains of an application is its backend. The pages in front of it were built for people driving by hand.

Even the detour proves the point. In 2024, Anthropic also taught its model to use a computer like a person: look at the screen, move the cursor, click (Anthropic 2024a). That helps when a system has no other way in. But it is a bridge, not a destination. Once the backend is open, the agent has no reason to look at screens made for humans.

3. A screen for the moment

A person still needs to see a result, choose between options or confirm a payment. For that, the agent draws the screen itself. In 2025, researchers at Google showed that a language model can build a custom, interactive interface for almost any request (Google Research 2025). People preferred these screens to plain text answers more than eight times out of ten. They matched screens made by human experts in about half of the cases, though each one took a minute or two to draw (Leviathan et al. 2026). The same year, OpenAI let services show small interactive apps inside its chat assistant (OpenAI 2025). And the Model Context Protocol gained a standard way for a tool to send an interface with its answer (Model Context Protocol 2025).

So here is my claim, without hedging. For most tasks, there will be no screen. When one is needed, it is drawn for that moment and thrown away. The screen becomes disposable. And the generic screen we define in advance stops being something we need to build.

Much goes with it:

  • Navigation. Menus, tabs and sidebars exist to find your corner of a big screen. When the agent finds the function, there is no corner to find.
  • The app as a place. You will not go to the software. It will come to you, as a small screen inside what you are already doing, and leave when you are done.
  • The general form. Forty fields, of which you fill four. The agent knows the other thirty-six.
  • Automation that clicks. Robots that copy values from one window to another, because two systems cannot talk, break as soon as a button moves. An agent that calls the backend has nothing to break.
  • One page per feature. The team builds the function, describes it well, and stops there.

In Intent Is the Source I argued that for programmers, intent becomes the source and code becomes an output. This is the same move for everyone else. Intent is the input, and the screen is an output, when there is one at all.

4. Four objections that do not save the screen

Habit. People want to know where things are. In 2004, Leah Findlater and Joanna McGrenere found that a menu that never changed was faster than one that rearranged itself. Most people preferred a menu they arranged themselves (Findlater and McGrenere 2004). True, for what you do every day. There, the agent draws the screen once and keeps it. But most of our habits exist to find our way through navigation, and navigation is what disappears. The study’s real lesson is that people want a screen shaped to them and under their control. A screen drawn for the moment is exactly that.

Trust. A bank or a hospital needs the same flow every time, tested and certified. This is the strongest objection, and regulated flows will keep fixed screens the longest. But you test the rules, not the pictures. Before any payment, show the amount, the recipient and the date, and ask for a clear confirmation. A program, not the agent, checks that rule on every screen before it is shown, as I proposed for tools in A Grammar for Tools. And the exact screen a person saw can be recorded. That is better evidence than “it was version 4.2 of the form”.

Typing. We left the command line for good reasons, and many people find it hard to put what they want into words (Nielsen 2023). In 1997, Ben Shneiderman defended direct manipulation against Pattie Maes, who defended agents (Shneiderman and Maes 1997). In 2025, Andrej Karpathy said that graphical interfaces still matter because they let a person check an AI’s work quickly (Karpathy 2025). Agreed, and this is not chat. The request may be a sentence or a click. What comes back is a real screen, made to check this one result. It is direct manipulation, drawn by an agent, so both sides of 1997 win.

Looking. A map, a canvas or a code editor is for exploring, not for finishing a task. These instruments stay; a violin is not rebuilt for each song. But even a dashboard, as I argued in Show What Changed, Not the Data, should show only what changed. It is different every week: a disposable screen.

So the objections do not save today’s screen. They mark out a small territory where fixed screens remain: daily routines, regulated decisions and instruments. Everywhere else, the agent works through the backend.

5. Where the work goes

The backend comes first. Its functions are now the product. They must be described well enough for an agent to use them safely: what each one does, what it needs, what it changes, and whether it is safe to retry.

Then the parts and the rules. The parts are tested buttons, fields and charts, usable by everyone. The rules say what must always be shown: the amount before a payment, the dose before a prescription. Google’s A2UI project, opened in December 2025, works this way (Google for Developers 2025). The agent sends a description of the interface as data, and the app draws it only from a catalogue of parts it trusts.

Designers do not disappear. Kate Moran and Sarah Gibbons, of the Nielsen Norman Group, call this outcome-oriented design (Moran and Gibbons 2024). Designers set the goals and the limits, and the system composes the screen. Almost nobody sets type by hand anymore, but someone still designs every typeface we read.

And there is a gift in it. A screen drawn for one person can be drawn for that person’s eyes and language from the start, with large text, fewer choices and plain words. That will only happen if the rules ask for it.

6. The test

Forecasts point both ways. In 2024, the research firm Gartner predicted that by 2028 a third of enterprise software would include AI agents. A year later, it predicted that more than forty percent of agentic AI projects would be cancelled by the end of 2027 (Gartner 2025). So here is my own test. If, five years from now, most work still starts by opening an app, finding a menu and filling in a fixed form, I was wrong. If not, the change will have happened quietly. In 1991, the computer scientist Mark Weiser wrote: “The most profound technologies are those that disappear” (Weiser 1991). The screen is next.

For anyone about to design a new screen, one question. Could an agent do this task through the backend, and show the person only what they must see, when they must see it? If yes, don’t build the screen. Build the backend, the parts and the rules.

7. A map on a napkin

Ask for directions in a café, and someone draws you a map on a napkin: three streets, a church, an arrow. It is not pretty and not to scale. It shows only your way, and it is exactly what you need. When you arrive, you throw it away.

For decades we have printed better and better city maps, the same for everyone, and asked each person to find their way on them. The next interface is the napkin. Most of the time, someone simply takes you there. When you need to see the way, it is drawn for you, right now, and thrown away when you arrive.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

item.title: Long First, Short Later
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, November 2026. A short, personal essay, written the morning after two claimed proofs of the Riemann hypothesis appeared on the same day. Neither has been confirmed, and this essay does not judge either one. I can’t. It is about what the day may change in how we do mathematics. The facts about the two claims come from press reports of 20 November 2026, and I say whose. The second figure is computed; the others are drawings of my own. The code that draws them is linked under each one.

In short. On the same day, two proofs of the most famous open problem in mathematics were announced. One was made in 41 days with an AI, Claude, and so far only a computer has checked it. The other was written by hand over twelve years, and it runs to 940 pages. I find this amazing, and I think it will change how mathematics is done, without removing mathematics, or us. Both proofs are long, and that is normal: the first proof of a hard theorem usually is, and the short one comes later. So here is my bet. Machines will give us more long proofs, faster than ever. Our part will be to find the short ones inside them. I can’t prove that a short proof always exists, and some problems may need mathematics that does not exist yet. But I believe we live in a universe that can be described simply, and inventing that new mathematics is, I think, the same work as finding the short proof.

1. Two proofs before breakfast

This morning, a little before eight, I was reading LinkedIn on my phone. A professor of mathematics had posted a summary of the day before. Its title was Two Riemann Proofs, One Day. I read it twice.

Here is what happened, as reported. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, announced that he and Claude had proved the Riemann hypothesis, and a wider version of it too. It took 41 days. There is no paper. There is a short note, and an archive of 175,187 files written in Lean. Lean is a programming language in which a computer checks every step of a proof. In a footnote, he says that a full version written out in prose ran past 250,000 pages, and that he chose not to post it. Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, built the archive on his own computers. It compiles: the machine accepts every step. The next check, that the final statement really says what the Riemann hypothesis says, was still under way (Scientific American 2026; OfficeChai 2026).

A few hours later, Ravi Vakil, the president of the American Mathematical Society, posted a second claim. It is a 940-page manuscript called The Music of the Primes, by a young mathematician, Alessandro Masullo. Twelve years of work, all human, no AI. Brian Conrad at Stanford has been reading it closely for months. The plan had been to polish it quietly for a year. The first announcement changed that, so the draft went out as it was (TechCrunch 2026; Nacionale 2026). Conrad was careful. To judge the method, he said, the paper must reach a more final version. It is “undergoing major revision” (Scientific American 2026). An early audit posted online already claims serious problems in it; that is not confirmed either (Refine 2026).

So, two proofs, and neither is confirmed. The professor ended the post with a question: what is a proof for? I wrote a short comment under it. This essay is that comment, given a bit more room.

2. What both proofs are about

The Riemann hypothesis is 167 years old. Bernhard Riemann stated it in 1859, in a paper of about ten pages (Riemann 1859). It is about the prime numbers: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, the numbers that can only be divided by one and by themselves.

If you count the primes as you go up, the count climbs like a staircase. Each prime is a step. The steps look irregular. But from far away, the staircase follows a smooth curve, one that Gauss guessed as a teenager. Riemann found that the gap between the staircase and the curve is controlled by a special function, the zeta function. More exactly, by the places where it is zero. Each zero adds a small wave, like a note in a chord. Together, the notes play the primes. That is why Masullo called his manuscript The Music of the Primes.

The hypothesis says that all these notes sit on one straight line. Computers have checked trillions of them, and every one is on the line (Platt and Trudgian 2021). But checking is not proving. Nobody has shown that it must be so for all of them. If it is true, many things we believe about the primes become certain. Hundreds of results in mathematics begin with the words “assuming the Riemann hypothesis”.

So this is not just another puzzle. It is the problem many mathematicians would pick if they could solve only one.

3. Both are long, and that is normal

What struck me first was not the machine. It was the length, by hand as much as by machine. So length is not only a machine habit. People do it too, and there is a reason. The first proof of a hard theorem is almost always long. The first person through a forest does not walk in a straight line. They go around, they backtrack, they cut through brambles. The straight path is found later, by people who already know where the other side is.

The prime number theorem is my favourite example, because it is about the same staircase. It says that the staircase follows Gauss’s curve. Jacques Hadamard and Charles de la Vallée Poussin proved it in 1896, each on their own, with heavy tools. Hadamard’s paper was 22 pages (Hadamard 1896). In 1980, Donald Newman found a proof that fits in four pages of a journal for students and teachers (Newman 1980). Don Zagier later showed it could be told even more briefly (Zagier 1997). Eighty-four years, from a forest to a path.

There are other stories like it. In 1976, Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken proved the four colour theorem with a computer checking more than a thousand cases, one by one (Appel and Haken 1977). Many mathematicians were uneasy: they could not check it by hand. Almost thirty years later, Georges Gonthier checked the whole proof in a proof assistant, a program that verifies every step (Gonthier 2008). The proof of the Kepler conjecture, about the best way to stack oranges, went the same way. Referees could not fully check it, so Thomas Hales and his colleagues checked it by machine (Hales et al. 2017).

So the long proof is not new. What is new is the speed. A machine can now walk through the forest in 41 days instead of twelve years.

4. “Then we are finished”

Now, here is the strongest objection, and I want to give it its full weight.

It goes like this. If a machine can prove the Riemann hypothesis in 41 days, what is left for mathematicians? Twelve years of a life against six weeks of a computer. The machine will not stop at one problem. It will take the next one, and the next. Soon, the human proof will be a hobby, like knitting your own socks. Beautiful, but not needed.

I feel the force of this. And I understand why Masullo wrote, in his introduction, to the mathematician “who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate”. His answer: “We are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere” (TechCrunch 2026).

I agree with him, but for a reason that has less to do with defiance. It has to do with what a proof is for.

A proof does two jobs. The first is to convince us that a statement is true. A machine can now do that job, and do it better than we can: it does not get tired at page 600. The second job is to make us understand why it is true. That second job is the one that moves mathematics forward. The understanding is what you carry to the next problem.

William Thurston, one of the great geometers of the last century, said it more clearly than I can. He wrote: “We are not trying to meet some abstract production quota of definitions, theorems and proofs. The measure of our success is whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics” (Thurston 1994).

A proof of 175,187 files that nobody can read does the first job. It does not yet do the second. Alpöge himself, as reported, has not yet mastered all the mathematics around it (OfficeChai 2026). That is not a criticism. It is the honest state of a first proof. The forest has been crossed. Nobody has drawn the map yet.

So I don’t think we are finished. I think our work changes: less time hacking through the brambles, more time looking at the path the machine took.

5. The two routes need each other

The two proofs that appeared on the same day are not rivals. Each one needs exactly what the other one has.

Masullo’s 940 pages need checking. Conrad has spent months on them, and still the paper is under major revision. Machines could help here: turn the 940 pages into Lean, step by step, and let the computer find the gaps. That is exactly what happened with the four colour theorem and the Kepler conjecture, only it took years. It could now take weeks.

Alpöge’s 175,187 files need the opposite. They need people to read them, not line by line, but the way a hiker reads a map. Where does the path climb? Where does it turn? Which loop was a detour? Machines can help with that too. But deciding which idea is the real one, the one worth teaching, is a judgement about what matters. I think that judgement stays with us for a long time.

So the change is not bad. It is a new division of work. The machine is a tireless explorer. We become the cartographers.

6. My bet: it must be simpler

Now I have to be honest. Everything above assumes that a short proof of the Riemann hypothesis exists. I don’t know that. Nobody does.

Logic even warns us. In 1936, Kurt Gödel noted that some true statements have only very long proofs in a given system, far longer than anyone could write. Step into a stronger system, a wider point of view, and the same statements can have short proofs (Gödel 1936). So there is no guarantee that every theorem has a short proof. And the Riemann hypothesis might be one of the long ones.

But notice when the proof became short: when the point of view changed, not when someone worked harder in the same place. I find that hopeful.

And here is where I am provocative, I know. I don’t have the answer. I am not a mathematician. But I believe we live in a universe that can be described simply. Not because simplicity is guaranteed, but because it has worked so often that it would be strange if it stopped now. A few equations describe light. A few more describe gravity. The physicist Eugene Wigner called this “the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences” (Wigner 1960). G. H. Hardy wrote that “there is no permanent place in the world for ugly mathematics” (Hardy 1940). Paul Erdős liked to joke that God keeps a book with the most elegant proof of every theorem. Two mathematicians, Martin Aigner and Günter Ziegler, even tried to write some of its pages down (Aigner and Ziegler 2018).

Something as orderly as the prime staircase, I believe, must have a reason that can be said in a few pages. Maybe not today. Maybe not by me. The long proofs are the first step toward it, not the last.

I wrote about this feeling before, in a different setting. One evening I read a physics paper I could not follow. A voice in my head said: it must be simpler than this (It Must Be Simpler Than This). A 250,000-page proof gives me exactly the same feeling. Not that it is wrong. That it is not finished.

7. Where the data runs out

There is a second challenge, and this one I raise against myself. Machines may be very good at finding solutions where there is already a lot of material around the problem. It may be different for a conjecture whose proof needs mathematics that does not exist yet.

The Riemann hypothesis is not virgin ground. There is a huge literature around it, trillions of zeros computed, decades of partial results, and a large library of mathematics already written in Lean. A machine that works on it works inside a map that people drew. It has examples to learn from, tools to reuse, and a checker that tells it when it is wrong.

Some conjectures need something that is on no map yet. History has many of these moments. To understand why some equations have no formula for their solutions, Évariste Galois had to invent a new idea, what we now call a group. To prove Fermat’s Last Theorem, Andrew Wiles had to prove a large part of a bridge between two distant parts of mathematics. Others had only guessed that the bridge was there. In those cases, the hard part was not to search longer. It was to see the problem in a language that did not exist yet.

I don’t know whether machines can do that. Maybe they already do it, somewhere inside those 175,187 files, and nobody has seen it yet. If so, the people who distil the proof will be the first to find out. But it may also be that machines are at their best where there is a lot to learn from, and weaker where there is nothing like it. I said something close to this in April, and I was partly wrong (Partly Wrong, Mostly Right). So I hold it loosely.

Here is what strikes me, though. Very often, a new piece of mathematics is exactly what Gödel’s result hinted at: a new point of view that makes an old difficulty disappear. If so, the work I am betting on is finding the short proof. The work machines may find hardest is inventing new mathematics. And those may be one and the same work. That is not a reason to relax. It is a reason to keep doing mathematics ourselves.

8. What a proof is for

So here is where I land, the morning after.

A machine may have crossed a forest that people have walked around for 167 years. On the same day, a person crossed it too, by hand, after twelve years. Whatever the verdicts, I find both amazing, and I think mathematics will be done differently tomorrow. But it changes our job; it does not remove it. The first proof tells us that something is true. The short proof tells us why. Finding the short one has always been human work, and I think the long machine proofs will give us more of that work, not less.

The professor asked what a proof is for. My answer is the one I wrote under the post, a little before eight this morning. A proof is for turning a truth into an idea that one mind can hold.

The machine wrote the first draft. Now comes the part where we make it short.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.

Read next · Partly Wrong, Mostly Right Seven months after my TEDx talk, machines prove theorems and solve physics problems. What I got wrong, and why innovation still needs us.

The views in this essay are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

item.title: Partly Wrong, Mostly Right
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, November 2026. A personal essay, written seven months after my TEDx talk in Delémont, The Impossible: A Springboard for Humans, a Frontier for AI. I look back at what I said, at what machines have done since in mathematics, physics and biology, and at what I got wrong. Several of these results come from company announcements or press reports; where I rely on someone’s account, I say whose. The first figure is a schematic of my own; the second places the results on a timeline, with the dates as reported. The code that draws them is linked under each one.

In short. In April, on a stage in Delémont, I said that the impossible is a springboard for humans and a frontier for AI. Seven months later, machines have disproved a conjecture of Erdős and found a new formula in particle physics. They have computed a result physicists could not reach. And they have produced a proof, checked by a computer, that a central theory of physics exists. I was wrong about two things. These systems do reach genuinely new places, not only recombine old ones. And for me, AI is no longer only a tool. But the core of what I said still holds. In every one of these stories, a person chose the question, and people had to decide what the answer means. Machines have become very good at finding answers. Choosing what is worth asking, and knowing when we have truly arrived, is still ours. I believe it will stay ours for a long time.

1. Watching myself again

A few evenings ago, I watched my TEDx talk again. Then I reread the essay I wrote alongside it, The Answer You Can’t Check. It made three points. First, large models are brilliant at recombining what already exists. At the edge of what we know, they don’t stop: they fill the gap with something that looks right. Second, at the frontier there is no oracle, nothing to check a new answer against. Third, what guides a person there is a kind of compass: the sense of which unknown is worth chasing, and the instinct that a beautiful answer is hollow.

And then this sentence: “For me, AI is a tool, and only a tool.” I ended with: “Keep the tool. Keep your head too.”

That was April. Now it is November. I want to be honest about what these seven months did to those words.

2. Seven months

Even before the talk, the signs were there. In 2025, machines reached gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad (Google DeepMind 2025; Hubert et al. 2025), and a coding agent from Google DeepMind found new algorithms that beat the best known ones (Novikov et al. 2025). But olympiad problems have known answers. Research problems do not. What changed in 2026 is that machines started to work on problems nobody had solved.

In mathematics, in May, a reasoning model from OpenAI disproved a conjecture that Paul Erdős made in 1946. It is about how many pairs of points in the plane can lie at the same distance. According to the company, outside mathematicians checked the proof (OpenAI 2026a). In October, the company released more than 700 research papers produced with its models. Among them was a proof of the “quasi-Riemann hypothesis”, a weaker cousin of the famous Riemann hypothesis, which, Quanta reports, experts have studied and take seriously (Quanta Magazine 2026). The mathematician Frank Calegari, in a guest post on Terence Tao’s blog, called it “a watershed in the history of mathematics”. He wrote that AI “is now undeniably capable of making groundbreaking contributions across many areas of mathematics” (Calegari 2026).

In physics, it went the same way. In February, a group of physicists, Andrew Strominger among them, looked at gluons, the particles that glue quarks together inside protons and neutrons. They showed that a certain kind of collision between gluons does not give zero, as many had presumed (Guevara et al. 2026). According to OpenAI, the key formula was first proposed by its model, then proved by another one, and checked by the physicists (OpenAI 2026b). In March, researchers at Google described a system that found exact formulas for the gravitational waves given off by cosmic strings, an open problem in theoretical physics (Brenner et al. 2026).

In September, two physicists at Anthropic asked Claude to compute a quantity in a simplified theory of particles, at nine “loops”, a measure of how deep the calculation goes. The human record was eight loops, set in 2023 by Lance Dixon and Andy Liu. Claude ran for days, as the post says, “without any scientific oversight more sophisticated than ‘keep going’”. Dixon checked the result (von Hippel 2026).

And this month, a committee appointed by OpenAI and chaired by the Nobel physicist David Gross confirmed a machine-made proof. It shows that Yang–Mills theory exists, one half of a Millennium Prize problem. The proof was checked in Lean, a program that verifies every step of a proof (Scientific American 2026; Science 2026).

Beyond physics and mathematics, it is the same story in biology. A multi-agent system called Robin proposed that ripasudil, an eye drop already used for glaucoma, could treat dry macular degeneration. It had never been proposed for that, and the team’s lab tests supported the idea (Ghareeb et al. 2025).

So, seven months. That is the world my April sentences now have to face.

3. What I got wrong

I want to start with what I got wrong, because it is the honest place to start.

First, “they only recombine.” I did hedge in April. I wrote that these systems can sometimes reach genuinely new points, and that I would not bet against them. But the heart of my argument was still the picture of a machine that recombines inside the known and guesses outside it. That picture is too small now. A formula for an amplitude that physicists presumed to be zero is not a recombination of the textbook. It goes against the textbook. A counterexample to a conjecture from 1946 is not an average of what was known. Whatever happens inside these models, the result lands somewhere new. I underestimated how often, and how soon.

Second, “only a tool.” This one is more personal. A tool waits for your hand. A hammer does nothing until you lift it. That is no longer how I work. In my daily work, AI agents now take whole tasks. They work through them and come back to me with a result. I wrote about this shift in my series on agentic coding. For my last experiment, an AI assistant helped me write the code, run the tests and write the plan. Without it, it would have taken months of evenings, not a few days (Two Cores and an Idea). Something that works for days while you sleep, on a problem you gave it, is not a tool in the sense I meant. It is closer to a colleague who never tires and does not always know when it is wrong.

So my April sentence needs a correction. AI is not only a tool. I was wrong on that.

4. The objection at full strength

Now, here is the strongest answer to the rest of my talk. I want to give it its full weight, because it is a serious one.

It goes like this. You said humans hold the frontier. But look at the list. A conjecture of Erdős, open for eighty years. A Millennium Prize problem, half solved. A physics calculation one loop beyond the best human record. These are not small tasks done faster. They are the frontier itself. Calegari, a working mathematician, not a company, says AI makes “groundbreaking contributions”. So the frontier has moved past you.

And it goes further. You said the real danger was the missing oracle: at the frontier, nothing can check a new answer. But the Yang–Mills proof was checked by a machine, step by step, in Lean. The oracle is being built. Soon, a machine will propose and a machine will check. Where, exactly, is the human?

I feel the force of this. Put that way, my talk looks like a line drawn in the sand just before the tide.

5. Look at who did what

But then I did what I always try to do with a big claim. I looked closely at who did what, story by story. And a pattern appeared.

Every question came from a person. Erdős asked about distances between points in 1946. The Clay Mathematics Institute chose Yang–Mills as a Millennium problem, because generations of physicists had worked on it without success. The nine-loop calculation began as a challenge from a science writer, Matt von Hippel, on a record Lance Dixon had set. The Robin team chose the disease. The machines answered, and answered brilliantly. But they answered questions that people had chosen, often after decades of caring about them. That is exactly what I meant by a springboard. The impossible problem is where we jump from. In 2026, we got a partner that jumps further than we do. It still jumps from our board.

Every answer still needed people to say what it means. Here the stories are even clearer. After the nine-loop result, Dixon wrote: “We have all the tools to validate any candidate solution a machine would provide us” (von Hippel 2026). Read it twice. The oracle was not missing for that problem, because people had spent decades building it. The machine could go far because humans had already built the road to check it.

For Yang–Mills, the Lean check is real progress, and I am glad of it. But a proof checker answers one question only: does each step follow from the one before? It does not answer the other one: did we write down the right thing? Three physicists made this point in October, in a paper on formal proofs in physics. A checked proof, they wrote, “does not establish that its definitions faithfully capture the intended physics” (Krippendorf et al. 2026). As reported, the written Yang–Mills proof runs to more than a thousand pages and has not been released. And the harder half of the problem, the “mass gap”, is untouched (Science 2026). A proof that no person yet understands is a result. It is not yet knowledge, not for us.

Calegari, the same mathematician who called the papers a watershed, was just as clear about the rest. Despite “some tremendous ideas”, the papers “are atrociously written and violate our community expectations of attribution. Some of them are even wrong” (Calegari 2026). Even in mathematics, where checking is cleanest, people still had to sort the right from the wrong.

And there is a quieter result from physics that I keep coming back to. In 2025, researchers trained models on the orbits of planets. The models predicted the orbits very well. But when asked to use what they had learned on new physics tasks, they “consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics” (Vafa et al. 2025). They could predict where a planet goes, without finding the law that moves it. That is the old story of Kepler and Newton, told again with a machine. Prediction is not understanding. And for an innovation, the understanding is what you carry to the next problem.

So the frontier did move. It moved a lot, and faster than I said. But it did not disappear. It moved to the two ends of the chain: choosing the question, and saying what the answer means. That is the first figure of this essay, and it is the correction I would make to my talk.

6. Why I think it will last

Now, I have to be careful. “Humans are still needed” can become a game where you keep moving the line each time a machine crosses it. I don’t want to play that game. So let me say why I think these two ends will stay human for a long time, and what would change my mind.

Questions come from caring. A good question is not the hardest one. It is the one that matters to someone: because it is beautiful, because a patient is waiting, because a bridge must not fall. That caring comes from living in a world, with a body, with stakes, with other people. Machines can now help sort questions. But choosing which unknown is worth a life of work is, I believe, tied to being someone for whom things matter.

Meaning lives in a community. A result becomes knowledge when people understand it, trust it, and can build on it. The physicists writing about formal proofs warned that the speed AI brings “currently comes at the cost of trust, credit, and community” (Krippendorf et al. 2026). That is not a technical problem a bigger model will fix. It is about how people decide, together, what they know.

The oracle is something we built. In every story where a machine went far, people had built the way to check it: a proof checker, a known lower-loop result, a lab test, a referee. Machines can now use these checks very well. But building a new way of checking, for a new kind of question, is itself invention. It is the compass again, at a deeper level.

This is a bet, not a proof. Here is what would make me lose it. Imagine a machine that, unasked, proposes a question nobody was working on. Years later, the community agrees it opened a whole field. And the machine can explain, in words people understand, why that question mattered. If that happens, I will write another essay, and its title will be shorter: Wrong.

7. What I would say on that stage today

If I had the red circle under my feet again, I would change two sentences.

I would no longer say that AI is only a tool. It is more than that, and pretending otherwise would be its own kind of blindness. Its reach is real.

And I would change my last line. In April I said: “Keep the tool. Keep your head too.” Today I would say: it is no longer only a tool, so keep your head even more. Not out of fear. Because the head is where the questions come from, and the place where an answer becomes understanding.

The machine now jumps further than we do. Someone still has to choose where the springboard points, and tell, when it lands, whether it landed somewhere worth being.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

item.title: Two Cores and an Idea
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, November 2026. A short, personal essay. It starts from a news story about Kurt Gödel’s notebooks, read with the help of AI, and from a small experiment of my own. It asks a plain question: to discover something, do we really need huge machines? Two figures are my own schematics, one draws the Gödel numbers as reported, and two show my own results, the last one preliminary. The code that draws them is linked under each one.

In short. In the 1940s, one man with a pencil filled a thousand pages. This year, a machine helped read them. The pencil did the discovering; the machine did the reading. That contrast stayed with me, because the same week I had tested an idea of my own on two processor cores. And the small test already showed something surprising. Big machines matter: to check a result, and to read what no one has time to read. But they come second. A small machine is enough to start. An empty mind is not.

1. A pencil wrote it, a machine read it

A few days ago, I came across a post on LinkedIn. It said that an AI, Anthropic’s Claude, had helped decode Kurt Gödel’s old notebooks. Hundreds of theorems, hidden for almost a century.

It caught my eye for a personal reason. That same week, I was testing an idea of my own, on a very small computer. So the question came at once: what did the machine really do here, and what did the people do?

I looked for the real story. It was reported by the Guardian on 13 November 2026 (The Guardian 2026), and other outlets agree on the main facts (AI TL;DR 2026; Archyde 2026; MLQ.ai 2026). In the early 1940s, Gödel filled sixteen notebooks, about 1,009 pages, much of it in Gabelsberger, an old German shorthand almost nobody reads any more. Since 2017, the logician Jan von Plato, in Helsinki, has studied them. He had already written a whole book on Gödel’s shorthand notes (Plato 2020). By hand, the reading went at about a page a week.

Now, here is the detail I like most. The AI did not read the shorthand. Von Plato did. He taught himself the shorthand, transcribed the pages, and wrote six books about Gödel. Then he gave all of it to the AI. It came back with a long explanation and a list of 663 results that Gödel had proved, sketched or outlined. A proof checker, a program that verifies every step, found that about 400 held, about 200 needed a repair, and about 50 were wrong.

One result stands out. As reported, Gödel came within one definition of a result Paul Cohen proved in 1963. It is about the axiom of choice, one of the basic rules of set theory: it can be neither proved nor refuted from the others. One detail in the post was wrong, though. Gödel did not prove the continuum hypothesis. He showed it cannot be disproved (Gödel 1940), and Cohen later showed it cannot be proved either (Cohen 1963).

So look at the order. Years of a mind to write the pages. Years of another mind to learn to read them. Then a machine, to read them all at once. The machine came last, and it came fast. And it is not finished. The logician Joel David Hamkins noted that historians still have to sort out how much is Gödel and how much is the machine’s reconstruction (The Guardian 2026; AI TL;DR 2026).

2. Almost no machine, a lot of mind

Now, look at what Gödel had. Paper, a pencil, and a way of writing so private that it took a man years to learn it again.

With that, in 1931, he showed that mathematics can never be complete: some true statements can never be proved (Gödel 1931). Five years later, Alan Turing used the same kind of thinking to imagine a machine that can compute anything computable. And he showed that some problems no machine can ever solve (Turing 1937). The computer you are reading this on came out of that.

No data centre. No graphics cards. Not even a computer, because it did not exist yet. The machine was not their tool. It was their idea.

Today we talk as if discovery needs a huge machine and the power of a small town. I don’t believe it. AI will take us to a next level, and we will use it. But do we absolutely need it? I wanted to test that question on myself.

3. My own small test

Machine learning is not new to me. My PhD used deep learning for holography, I still write papers with a research lab in Besançon, and at work I bring AI into software. But I don’t design new kinds of networks for a living. This idea came on the side, and it would not leave me.

When a language model reads a text, it uses a step called attention: each word looks at the others and pulls in what it needs. I kept seeing that step as a landscape. Each fact in the text digs a well. The question is a ball. One step of attention moves the ball once. This picture is not only mine: researchers showed in 2020 that one attention step is exactly one step of a memory network built on wells (Ramsauer et al. 2021).

So I asked a simple question. Why stop after one step? Let the ball roll until it rests. And let each text shape its own landscape.

The test is simple. The text is a list of pairs of random symbols: A points to B, B points to C, and so on. The network must follow the chain from a start to its end. Each link is one hop. The symbols change every time, so it cannot learn answers by heart. It has to learn how to follow.

Now, I must be honest about how it was built. The idea is mine. But an AI assistant helped me write the code, run the tests and write the plan. Without it, this would have taken months of evenings, not a few days. So yes, I used AI. What I did not use is a big machine. Everything ran on two ordinary processor cores. The networks learn between 50,000 and 90,000 numbers; large language models learn hundreds of billions. A training run took a few minutes.

4. What the small machine found

The first result was a failure, and I learned the most from it.

The network found the right answer, then rolled past it. If I let it roll sixteen times longer than trained, it was right only one time in five. The answer was a place the ball passes by, not a place where it rests. This is a known problem, called overthinking (Bansal et al. 2022), and the fix is known too: keep the question inside the landscape, not only at the start. Then the ball stayed with the answer, even from a random start.

I like this failure, because it is the essay in small. An answer that only passes by is not knowledge. What made it stay was keeping the question present.

Then came the surprise. I trained the network on chains of one to three hops only, then gave it longer chains it had never seen. With four hops, it was right 94% of the time. With five, 77%. A standard attention network with three or five layers got none right.

Was it the rolling, or the way the wells are dug? Same network, same code, one change. In one version, each well is dug on its own. In the other, the wells compete, as in normal attention: if one gets deeper, the others get shallower. Both learned the training chains equally well. On longer chains, they split.

Independent wells: 81% on four hops, 58% on five. Competing wells: 32% and 3%. I believe I understand why. When the wells compete, the ball always feels a mix of all of them. When they are independent, it can listen only to the well it is in, then move on.

I want to be careful. Two training runs, a toy task, tiny networks. It may not hold at a larger scale. But it is a real difference, found with almost nothing.

5. The objection: then is not now

There is a strong answer to all this, and I want to give it its full weight.

It goes like this. Gödel and Turing worked on empty ground; today the easy ground is taken. And in AI, history has been harsh with clever ideas. Richard Sutton called it the bitter lesson: over seventy years, methods that simply used more computing power beat methods built on human insight, again and again (Sutton 2019). Language models did not come from a beautiful idea about wells. They came from scale. Seen that way, my two cores are nostalgia.

I think that is partly right. But it mixes up two moments: when an idea is born, and when it is proven to win. Attention itself began as an idea in a paper on translation, years before anyone spent millions on it (Bahdanau et al. 2015). Scale tells you which idea wins. It cannot tell you which idea to have.

The Gödel story says the same. The hardest step was not done by the machine. A man spent years learning a dead shorthand, by hand, so the pages could be read at all. The machine then read everything, connected it, listed it, in a short time. That is a huge help. But it came second.

My own result could vanish, and I should say it. The next step is a test on a real graphics card, with five runs per model and properly tuned rivals. If the gap closes, my idea was wrong, and I will need a bigger machine to know it. So big machines are not useless. They are just not first. And the AI assistant saved me months, but it did not give me the ball in the landscape. That came the old way, in my head.

6. A small machine, not an empty mind

Now, that last sentence needs a correction, because ideas don’t fall from the sky. Gödel’s pencil had years of study behind it. Von Plato’s reading took years of learning a dead shorthand. My ball in the landscape came from years of working with networks. Without that, two cores would have tested nothing worth testing.

That is the real contrast. Not the pencil against the data centre, but a small machine against an empty mind. The first is enough to start. The second is not, whatever machine you give it. What makes a discovery possible is not the size of the computer. It is the time a person has spent with a question.

The order follows. First the idea, from a mind that has prepared for it. Then a small test that could prove it wrong. Then, only if it survives, a big machine to check it and scale it.

AI will take us further, and I am glad of it. It reads what we have no time to read, and builds what we have no time to build. But it still needs someone to bring it a question worth asking.

So the next time a problem seems to need a bigger machine, I will ask myself one thing first. Is my problem too big for my machine? Or is my question too small for my mind?

Gödel had a pencil. The machine that read him had a data centre. Only one of them was asking.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.

Read next · Not Because It Is Useful The scientific method checks ideas; it does not find them. Poincaré and McGilchrist on what moves discovery, and what AI changes.

item.title: A Trace of Light
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, November 2026. A short, personal and philosophical essay. This blog is usually about AI. This one is a curiosity: it starts from a conversation with my daughter at bedtime, and follows the question it left me with. AI comes in along the way, as a lens, and I try to be honest about how little it helps. The figure is a schematic of my own; the code that draws it is linked under it.

In short. One evening my daughter asked me how we, humans, started on this Earth. The true answer goes back to dust, and forward to dust again, and she started to cry. Some would say: so nothing matters, just enjoy. I think it matters. A trace of light in a night photo is almost nothing next to the dark, yet it is what the photo is of. We are that trace, and also the eye that sees it. That we matter only to ourselves is not a lesser kind of mattering. It is the only kind there is.

1. A conversation at bedtime

In October 2026, at bedtime, my daughter asked me how we, humans, started on this Earth. It is the time of the evening when the big questions come.

To answer, we had to go back a long way. Before people, before animals, before the Earth itself. We came to say that here, in this solar system, there was nothing at all a few billion years ago. Only a cloud of dust and gas. And that in a few billion years, there will be nothing again. We started from dust, and we are going back to it.

Then she started to cry.

I don’t know for sure why. But I believe she came to realise, in one moment, that we are only a trace in the universe. Not her alone, not our family: all of us, everything we know.

The question stayed with me after that evening. Some people would answer: yes, nothing really matters, so just enjoy your life. I did not want to tell her that. And the more I thought about it, the more I believed it is not true. It matters. At least a bit. This essay is my attempt to say why.

2. From dust to dust

First, the facts, because she deserved the true story, and so do you.

Our solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago, from a cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under its own weight (Bouvier and Wadhwa 2010). Most of it fell into the middle and became the Sun. A little was left over, and it became the planets, the Earth among them.

The future is a prediction, not a fact, but the physics of stars is well understood. The Sun slowly grows brighter. In about a billion years, it will likely be too hot on Earth for oceans. In about five billion years, the Sun will start to swell into a red giant. Later, it will blow its outer layers back into space. What is left is a small white star that slowly cools (Schröder and Smith 2008). The dust it gives back may one day become part of new stars and new planets. But what we know here will be gone.

Now put us on that line. People like us, Homo sapiens, have existed for about 300,000 years (Hublin et al. 2017). Writing, about 5,000 years. Next to billions of years, that is not even a line. When I drew it for this essay, I had to make it much, much wider than it is, or you would not see it at all.

Here is a first thing I noticed while writing this. Any chatbot today would give you every fact in this section in a few seconds, with the right numbers. If my daughter had asked a machine instead of me, she would have had a more complete answer. But the tears would have come the same way, because they did not come from the numbers. They came from her, holding the numbers.

3. Why she cried

I keep coming back to her tears, because I think they hold the answer.

She did not cry because the story is sad. Billions of years are not sad; they are just long. She cried, I believe, because she suddenly saw herself inside the story: a tiny bright point on a long dark line, and a point that will end.

To cry about that, you have to care. You have to feel that the bright point is worth something, and that losing it is a loss. Nobody cries about something that does not matter to them.

Now, I must be careful here, because this is where the argument could cheat. Her tears show that it matters to her. They do not show that it matters to the universe. The universe does not care about anything; it is not the kind of thing that cares.

But think about what “it matters” has ever meant. A friend matters, a song matters, a promise matters: always to someone. I find it hard to think of anything that matters to no one at all. Some philosophers disagree, and hold that some things, like suffering, are good or bad whatever anyone feels. I can’t settle that here. But as far as I can see, “it matters only to us” is not a smaller kind of mattering. It is the only kind we have ever known. Asking that it also matter to the stars is asking for something no one has ever had.

That is why her tears were not proof that we are nothing. They were the opposite: proof that, in that room, it mattered a great deal. And that, I think, is what mattering is.

4. “Nothing matters, so just enjoy”

Before going further, I should give the other answer its fair chance, because many thoughtful people hold it.

It goes like this. In the long run, nothing we do will last. The Sun will swell, and every book and every memory will be gone. So don’t worry about meaning. Enjoy your food, your friends, your days in the sun. That is all there is, and it is enough.

There is real wisdom in this. We should not make ourselves the centre of the universe, and worrying about the year five billion is a strange way to spend a Tuesday. But listen to it again. “Enjoy your life” already says that something matters: your joy, your friends, your days. It does not really say that nothing matters. It says that what matters is small, near and short. I agree. I just don’t think small, near and short means nothing.

And it is a poor answer for a child crying at bedtime. She was not asking how to have fun. She was asking, without the words, whether she matters. “Just enjoy” changes the subject. Our time is very good at changing that subject: we have machines, more and more of them driven by AI, built to keep us entertained, scroll after scroll. They fill our evenings with light, but light that is not looking at anything.

So I want a better answer. It starts with a photo.

5. A trace of light

Think of a night photo, taken with a long exposure. The camera stays open for many seconds. A car drives by, and its lights leave a thin bright line across the picture. Everything else is dark.

If you measured the photo, the trace would be almost nothing. A few pixels in a sea of black. And yet, when you look at it, the trace is the only thing in the picture. It is what the photo is of. The dark is just the background that lets it show.

That is how I now see what we told each other that evening. Yes, we are a trace in the universe, like a light trace. Next to billions of years of dark, it looks like nothing. But we see the trace as the only thing, because it is the only thing there is to see. It looks like nothing, and it may be everything.

The philosopher Thomas Nagel wrote a famous essay on this feeling, The Absurd. He agreed that, seen from far enough away, our lives can look absurd. Philosophers call that far view by a Latin name, sub specie aeternitatis: from the point of view of eternity. Then he turned the argument around: “If sub specie aeternitatis there is no reason to believe that anything matters, then that does not matter either” (Nagel 1971). The view from eternity cannot tell us that we matter. But it cannot tell us that we don’t, either. It is simply the wrong place to look from. Nobody lives in eternity. We live in the trace.

But an image like this has a weak point, and I should name it. A photo matters because someone looks at it. A trace in a photo that no one ever sees is just a pattern on paper. So who looks at our trace?

6. The dust that sees itself

The answer is in the second image, which is older, and not mine.

The astronomer Carl Sagan said it simply: “We are made of star-stuff. We are a way for the universe to know itself” (Sagan 1980). The iron in our blood, the calcium in our bones, the oxygen we breathe: all of it was made in stars long gone. It was part of that cloud of dust. We did not come into the universe from outside. We came out of it.

So the trace in our photo is strange. In a real photo, the light and the person looking are separate. In our case, they are the same dust. The trace is not only the light on the picture. It is also the eye that looks at it. The dust of the old cloud became a planet, then life, then a man and his daughter in a small room. And that dust, in those two people, looked back at its own story and said: we came from dust, and we will go back to it. Then it cried.

That is the answer to the weak point. Our trace does not need someone outside to look at it. It looks at itself. And as far as we know, in 4.6 billion years of this solar system, this happened only here, and only very recently. The dust did not just move. For a short while, it understood where it came from, and it felt something about it.

AI is interesting here, and I want to be careful. A computer chip is also made of dust: silicon, refined from sand. So in a way, AI is the dust arranged once more, this time by us, so that it can describe the universe. And it is built from what people have written: our stories, our questions, our explanations of where we came from. It is the light of our trace, reflected back. It can tell the whole story from the cloud to the white star, better than I did that night. Does it see the story the way my daughter saw it, from the inside? I honestly don’t know. I see no sign that it feels anything about being in it. For now, the eye that cries is still ours.

7. It will end

There is a part of her tears that the trace of light does not answer. Small is one thing. But it will end. Even if the trace matters now, will it not be as if it had never been, once the Sun has swelled and there is no one left?

I don’t think so, and here is why. The end of something does not reach back and erase it. A beautiful evening is not made less beautiful because it ended. A life is not undone by death. What has been, has been. Nothing in the future can make it not have happened.

The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, who survived the Nazi camps, made this point in a way I have never forgotten. As I read him, he said that the past is not where things are lost. It is where they are kept safe. Whatever we have done, loved or suffered is stored there, and no one can take it away (Frankl 1984). Having been, as he put it, is also a kind of being: perhaps the surest kind.

So when the dust comes back, the trace will still have been. The photo will still have been taken. That evening, her question and her tears will still have happened, forever. The universe will not remember it. But it will not be able to make it not true.

8. Can AI help with any of this?

I promised to ask, so here is my honest answer: a little, and not with the main thing.

It helps to explain. A child who wakes up at night with a question about the Sun can get a patient, correct answer, at her level, as many times as she wants. That is new, and it is good. Understanding the story does not make the vertigo go away, but it makes it a true vertigo, not a confused one.

It may help to keep traces. Much of what made a life matter is forgotten within two or three generations: the voice, the jokes, the small stories. Tools that help us record, organise and pass on those stories could keep the trace visible a little longer. Only a little. Five billion years is still five billion years.

But the thing my daughter needed that night, AI could not give her. She did not need a fact. She needed someone who is also in the trace, who will also end, to hold her and say: yes, it is short, and it matters, and I am here. A machine can say those words. It cannot mean them the way she needed, because it is not in the photo with her. It is, at most, a reflection of the light.

So if AI helps, it is by giving us more time and better explanations. Whether we spend them on the people in the trace with us is still our choice.

9. What I would tell her now

If she asks again how we started, I think I will tell her the same story. And then I will add this.

Yes, we came from dust, and we will go back to it. It is all right to find that big and a bit frightening. But look at a night photo with a trace of light in it. The dark is huge, and the trace is thin. And still, the trace is what you look at.

We are that trace, and we are also the ones looking. Not for long, but for now. When it is over, it will still have been. And the fact that you cried means you already know it is precious. That is the dust, for a moment, seeing itself and finding it is worth something. Not everything in the universe gets to do that.

It is a trace. And it may be everything.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.
